summary: A status report on the network numbers and autonomous system numbers used in the Internet community.

eli5.summary: Every network has a number, like a street number. This is a list of who had which numbers at the time.

questions: what are class a b and c networks
how many class b networks are there
subtitle: A 1990 snapshot of who held which Internet network numbers and autonomous system numbers.

tldr.problem: Every network on the Internet needs a unique number, and every group of gateways that exchanges routes needs its own identifier. Someone has to keep the list so numbers are not handed out twice.
tldr.mechanism: This memo lists every assigned network number (classes A, B and C) and autonomous system number, with a code for the kind of user and a reference to the person responsible. It also explains how the 32-bit address splits into classes.
tldr.outcome: It is a dated status report, not a protocol: the list was meant to be updated periodically, and current information came from Hostmaster at the DDN Network Information Center. The RFC is Informational and was later updated by RFC 5737.

today: RFC 1166 is an Informational RFC from July 1990 and is updated by RFC 5737. It obsoletes RFC 1020, RFC 1062 and RFC 1117, and it was a snapshot meant to be refreshed periodically, so its listings describe 1990 rather than the present.

sections.title: What This Memo Records
sections.content:
RFC 1166 documents the currently assigned network numbers and gateway autonomous systems. It says that it will be updated periodically, and that current information can be obtained from Hostmaster at the DDN Network Information Center (NIC) at SRI International.

Each entry names the registered network or system and gives a bracketed reference such as [nn,iii]. The number cites a document and the letters cite the NIC Handle of the responsible person. A NIC Handle is a unique identifier used in the NIC WHOIS/NICNAME service, and the memo points readers there for current mailboxes and phone numbers.

The text lists RFC 1117 and RFC 1020 among the many earlier documents it obsoletes. The memo also notes that most Internet protocols are documented in the RFC series, but that some of the items listed are undocumented.
sections.eli5: It is a directory. Each line says which network has which number and who to call about it.

sections.title: Address Classes
sections.content:
The network numbers are used as internet addresses by the Internet Protocol (IP). IP uses a 32-bit address field and divides it into a network part and a "rest" or local address part. The division takes four forms, called classes.

  • Class A: a 7-bit network number and a 24-bit local address; the highest-order bit is 0. This allows 128 class A networks.
  • Class B: a 14-bit network number and a 16-bit local address; the two highest-order bits are 1-0. This allows 16,384 class B networks.
  • Class C: a 21-bit network number and an 8-bit local address; the three highest bits are 1-1-0. This allows 2,097,152 class C networks.
  • Class D: a multicast address; the four highest-order bits are 1-1-1-0.

No addresses are allowed with the four highest-order bits set to 1-1-1-1. These are called "class E" and are reserved.
sections.eli5: An address is like a street number plus a house number. Some towns are huge with many houses, and some are tiny, so there are a few different sizes of address.

sections.title: How the Listings Are Written
sections.content:
The memo uses dotted decimal notation, which splits the 32-bit address into four 8-bit fields written as decimal numbers separated by periods. The example given is VENERA.ISI.EDU, written 128.009.000.032 or 128.9.0.32.

In the listings, nnn stands for part or all of a network number and rrr for part or all of a local address. A class A network therefore looks like nnn.rrr.rrr.rrr, a class B like nnn.nnn.rrr.rrr and a class C like nnn.nnn.nnn.rrr.

A one-character code at the left of each entry shows the kind of user: R for Research, D for Defense, G for Government (non-defense) and C for Commercial. An asterisk before the number marks an independent network. Independent networks must apply separately for permission to interconnect with the Internet and should not be listed in the working tables of Internet hosts or gateways. A number that has changed is kept for a transition period as an "old number" entry marked T, with the name suffixed -TEMP.
sections.eli5: The list uses a little code: a letter says who owns the network, a star means it is a separate club, and TEMP means the number is being changed.

sections.title: Special Addresses
sections.content:
Some addresses carry fixed meaning rather than naming a specific host. An address of zero means "this", as in "this network": the example is that 0.0.0.37 could be read as host 37 on this network. An address of all ones means "all", as in all hosts: 128.9.255.255 could be read as all hosts on network 128.9.

The class A network number 127 is assigned the loopback function. A datagram sent by a higher level protocol to a network 127 address should loop back inside the host, and no datagram "sent" to a network 127 address should ever appear on any network anywhere.

The listing also reserves 224.000.000.000-239.255.255.255 for multicast and 240.000.000.000-255.255.255.255 as reserved.
sections.eli5: Some numbers are special. One means "this place", one means "everybody", and one, 127, means "myself", so a message sent there never leaves the computer.

sections.title: The Network Number Registry
sections.content:
The bulk of the memo (it runs to 182 pages) is tables. They cover class A, class B and class C networks, each row giving the code, the address range, the network name and the reference. Many rows are marked Unassigned or Reserved, and some ranges, such as 128.64.rrr.rrr-128.79.rrr.rrr, are listed as one unassigned block.

A few class A entries show the flavour of the list: network 10 is ARPANET, network 26 is MILNET and network 44 is AMPRNET. Network 127 is Loopback and network 0 is Reserved. Class B entries start at 128.0 (Reserved) and class C entries at 192.0.0 (Reserved).

Network numbers are assigned for networks connected to the research Internet and the operational Internet, and for independent networks that use the IP family protocols, which the memo says are usually commercial.
sections.eli5: Most of the document is one huge list, like a phone book. Each line pairs a network number with its name and a person to contact.

sections.title: Network Totals
sections.content:
A short section counts the numbers by class and by user category. For networks assigned for the ARPA-Internet and the DDN-Internet it reports 29 class A, 1209 class B and 2972 class C networks, 4210 in all. For numbers allocated for Internet and independent uses together, the totals are 34, 2533 and 16214, or 18781 in all.

A third table gives the maximum allowed, for example 126 class A networks, 16382 class B networks and 2097150 class C networks, 2113658 in total. Comparing the tables shows how much of the space was still unassigned in July 1990.
sections.eli5: The memo also counts how many numbers were used and how many are still left, like counting the empty seats in a theatre.

sections.title: Autonomous System Numbers
sections.content:
The Exterior Gateway Protocol (EGP) specifies that groups of gateways may form autonomous systems. EGP provides a 16-bit field for identifying such systems, and the values of this field are registered in this memo.

The table lists each number, a system name and a contact. Number 1 is The BBN Core Gateways, 2 is DCN-AS, 3 is The MIT Gateways and 4 is ISI-AS, and the list continues through hundreds of numbers, ending with entries named CANET-AS in the 600s.
sections.eli5: Groups of routers that work together as one team get a team number. This part of the list says which team has which number.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The memo's security section is a single sentence: security issues are not discussed in this memo. The final pages carry the Documents list (the references behind the bracketed numbers), the Contacts list of NIC Handles with names and mailboxes, and the authors' addresses at SRI International.
sections.eli5: The memo does not talk about keeping things safe. It is just a list.
